claims.claim: An AWS access key consists of an access key ID and a secret access key that must be used together; the secret can be retrieved only at creation.
claims.locator: Access keys consist of two parts

claims.claim: AKIA is the prefix of an access key and ASIA of a temporary (AWS STS) access key ID; AIDA is an IAM user and AROA a role.
AKIA keys are long-term credentials for an IAM user or root user; ASIA keys are temporary credentials created with AWS STS.
An IAM user can have a maximum of two access keys.
claims.locator: You can have a maximum of two access keys per user.

claims.claim: Anyone who has your access keys has the same level of access to your AWS resources that you do.
claims.locator: First sentence of Secure access keys

claims.claim: userIdentity.accessKeyId is the access key ID that was used to sign the request; type values include IAMUser and AssumedRole.
Secret scanning scans the entire Git history on all branches, also issues, pull requests, discussions and wikis; it runs automatically and free on public repositories; partners are notified.
claims.locator: Secret scanning scans your entire Git history on all branches

claims.claim: Push protection blocks pushes containing recognised secrets; bypass reasons are used in tests, false positive, fix later; a bypass is added to the audit log.
Audit log actions secret_scanning_alert.create, secret_scanning_alert.public_leak, secret_scanning_push_protection.bypass and repo.access with the stated meanings.
Alert fields state (open, resolved), validity (active, inactive, unknown), publicly_leaked, multi_repo, push_protection_bypassed, first_location_detected with path, start_line, commit_sha.
claims.locator: Response schema of the alert endpoints

claims.claim: OpenAI advises never deploying a key in client-side environments like browsers or mobile apps; AWS advises not embedding access keys in a mobile app even in encrypted storage.
claims.locator: Never deploy your key in client-side environments like browsers or mobile apps

claims.claim: T1552.001 names source code with embedded passwords and files such as ~/.aws/credentials; T1593.003 mentions accidentally leaked credentials or API keys.
LLMjacking was named by Sysdig; the first case took credentials from a system running vulnerable Laravel (CVE-2021-3129) and targeted ten AI services, listed by name.
Worst-case cost 46,080 USD per day: 500,000 tokens per minute, 0.016 USD per 1,000 tokens average (0.008 input, 0.024 output), 60 x 24, four Regions.
Follow-up report: over 100,000 USD per day with newer models; more than 85,000 Bedrock requests, 61,000 in a three-hour window.
T1496.004 Cloud Service Hijacking is in the Impact tactic and its description names LLMJacking with reverse proxies.
LLM10:2025 is Unbounded Consumption and describes denial of wallet through a high volume of operations exploiting the cost-per-use model.
Bedrock logs InvokeModel, InvokeModelWithResponseStream, Converse and ConverseStream as management events; management events are logged by default and data events are not.
claims.locator: Amazon Bedrock management events in CloudTrail

claims.claim: The access check was InvokeModel with max_tokens_to_sample set to -1, producing ValidationException; without access the error would be AccessDenied; errorMessage max_tokens_to_sample: range: 1..1,000,000.
GetModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration was used to check logging; CloudTrail does not capture prompts or responses.
ListFoundationModels and GetFoundationModelAvailability were used to enumerate models before use.

Attackers called PutFoundationModelEntitlement (usually with PutUseCaseForModelAccess) and DeleteModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration; disabled models are not a security measure; Converse produces no InvokeModel CloudTrail logs.
claims.locator: API calls named in the article

claims.claim: Observed user agent Python/3.11 aiohttp/3.9.5; Regions attempted in the first report: us-east-1, us-west-2, ap-southeast-1, ap-northeast-1, eu-central-1, eu-west-3, us-gov-west-1.
Streaming operations write an additional stream-completion event with eventType AwsServiceEvent, same eventName, identity, address and user agent; count only AwsApiCall.
Namespace AWS/Bedrock; metrics Invocations, InputTokenCount, OutputTokenCount, InvocationClientErrors, InvocationThrottles; throttled requests are not counted in Invocations; ModelId dimension.
Token counts inputTokens and outputTokens sit under serviceEventDetails; serviceEventDetails.parentRequestId equals the requestID of the API call.
Model invocation logging is disabled by default; record fields identity.arn, modelId, input.inputTokenCount, output.outputTokenCount; bodies up to 100 KB.
Anthropic usage data comes in 1m, 1h or 1d buckets, can be filtered and grouped by API key, workspace and model, and typically appears within 5 minutes.
claims.locator: Usage API key concepts and FAQ

claims.claim: UpdateAccessKey changes the status from Active to Inactive or back; Inactive means the key cannot be used.
Rotation: create a second key, update applications, check last used, set the old key Inactive, confirm, delete; a deactivated key can be reactivated.
claims.locator: To update access keys without interrupting your applications

claims.claim: GetAccessKeyLastUsed returns the date and time of last use with the service and Region of the last request.
AWS advises different access keys for different applications, IAM policy conditions for expected networks, and temporary credentials instead of long-term keys.
claims.locator: Manage IAM user access keys properly

claims.claim: AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantineV2 is applied by the AWS team when credentials are compromised or exposed publicly, must not be removed, and denies bedrock:InvokeModel, bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream and bedrock:PutFoundationModelEntitlement among others.
An Anthropic API key has a status that an administrator can set to active, inactive or archived.
LLM10:2025 lists Rate Limiting among its prevention and mitigation strategies.
repo.access means the visibility of a repository changed and carries visibility and previous_visibility.
The stages and event names of the pattern (list calls, failing InvokeModel, logging check, entitlement, four invocation operations, logging deletion).
claims.locator: API calls named in the article

claims.claim: Stream-completion records carry inputTokens and outputTokens under serviceEventDetails with eventType AwsServiceEvent.
CloudTrail values for the access-check record: eventSource bedrock.amazonaws.com, errorCode ValidationException, errorMessage text, modelId anthropic.claude-v2, readOnly true.

quiz_map.support: A key ID that starts with AKIA is a long-term access key that stays valid until someone revokes it.
An active key is an incident, not a hygiene note.
The figure assumes the whole token quota is used every minute of the day in four Regions.
A ValidationException on such a call proves the key may invoke the model, because a key without permission would get AccessDenied instead.
A Converse call is recorded under its own event name and produces no InvokeModel record.
A stream-completion event is not an API call, so count invocations only where eventType is AwsApiCall.
Deactivate first, then rotate, then delete.
The Converse calls from a first-seen address in a Region the team never uses are what move this from exposure to confirmed abuse.
An ID that starts with AKIA is a long-term key that works until a person revokes it.
A repository that changes from private to public exposes every secret in its history at that moment.
A validity of active means the key still works, so treat the alert as an incident.
Deleting the line in a later commit does not help, because the key stays in the history.
A ValidationException on a deliberately invalid request shows the key is allowed to invoke the model, because a key without permission gets AccessDenied.
The same access key ID appearing from an address it has never used before is the strongest single signal.
To follow one caller through the log, search for the access key ID in userIdentity.accessKeyId.
In order, the caller enumerates models, checks access, checks logging, enables models and invokes at volume, and the bill follows.
Switches on a model the account had not enabled
In order, the caller enumerates models, checks access, checks logging, enables models and invokes at volume, and the bill follows.
A spike is authorised when the key, the source address, the model and a change ticket all match what the team planned.
Pivot on the access key ID, not on the user name, because one IAM user can hold two keys.
Deactivate the key first, because an Inactive key cannot be used but can be switched back to Active if a real application breaks.
